profile.reading:
Lincoln Rackhouse Maryland is a data center at 12401 Prosperity Drive in Silver Spring, Maryland, roughly fifteen miles north of Washington, D.C. The facility sits on about fifteen acres and occupies a single story building of 214,000 square feet, split between 90,000 square feet of raised technical floor and 37,000 square feet of office and flex space. According to the operator's own materials, the building can support up to 4.7 megawatts of critical IT load, with roughly 2 megawatts available for new customers at the time the page was published. Power arrives on dual feeds from diverse 25kV substations, and standby power is provided by ten 2.25 megawatt diesel generators arranged in an N plus one configuration, backed by twenty eight 750 kVA uninterruptible power supply units. The site is built to support N plus one, N plus two, or fully redundant two N configurations depending on a customer's requirements.

Cooling is handled by two high temperature chilled water central plants that the operator describes as fully mechanically redundant, supported by a 135,000 gallon thermal storage tank and 315,000 gallons of makeup water storage, a setup meant to keep cooling running through a utility interruption without immediately depending on generators. Fire protection uses a dual pre-action dry pipe system, which is common in raised floor data halls because it reduces the risk of accidental water discharge near electronic equipment.

The building is marketed as carrier neutral, with more than twenty metro carriers available and named Tier 1 providers including AT&T, Comcast, Zayo, Lumen, and Verizon connecting on site through two separate meet me rooms. Physical security includes twenty four hour staffed guarding, a K-4 rated crash resistant perimeter fence, biometric access readers, and continuous video surveillance, and the operator describes the facility as built to Tier III standards.

The property is operated by Lincoln Rackhouse, the data center investment and development arm of Lincoln Property Company, a large national commercial real estate firm. That parentage is typical of the Rackhouse portfolio, which leases wholesale and colocation space in existing large format buildings rather than building single tenant campuses from scratch. Beyond the specifications published on the operator's own site, no additional detail on the building's construction date, prior use, or current tenant roster is publicly available, which is standard practice for a wholesale colocation asset where tenant identities are typically confidential.
profile.research_note: Operator page: "214,000 SF Single Story Existing Building", "90,000 SF Raised Floor", "4.7 MW of critical IT load available", standby power via "Ten (10) 2.25 MW backup generators" (22.5 MW total). Page also references unrelated Plano, TX content in one section (apparent template/content-merge artifact on the operator's own site) -- the numeric specs quoted here are the ones explicitly tied to the Silver Spring, MD address on the same page.
profile.square_footage: 214,000 SF (90,000 SF raised floor, 37,000 SF office/flex space)

reading.body:
Lincoln Rackhouse Maryland, a single-story facility in Silver Spring totaling 214,000 square feet, publishes 4.7 MW of critical IT load currently deployed. Of this, 2 MW remains available for new customers. At a common AI training density of 40 kW per rack, the current deployed load represents roughly 118 racks, though this figure depends on actual customer configurations and is not the operator's stated capacity metric.

The facility is backed by ten 2.25 MW backup generators, providing 22.5 MW of generation capacity. This redundancy ratio suggests the site is engineered for sustained operation, though published specifications do not detail grid connection capacity, primary power terms, or how the gap between generator capacity and IT load is bridged during normal operation.

Lincoln Rackhouse Maryland ranks first among three facilities with published megawatt figures in Maryland. The state has 11 mapped facilities total. This single campus accounts for roughly half of Maryland's 9.3 MW of published IT load capacity, making it the largest disclosed facility in the state by that metric.
